# Story Structure

## Fractal Kishōtenketsu

> status: ratified (D-0044, D-0055, D-0210)

The four-beat, twist-not-clash structure (ki → shō → ten → ketsu) operates
fractally wherever the material earns it: across the four-act series, within acts,
multi-episode arcs, episodes, scenes, and smaller artifacts. It must not be imposed
where it makes a unit incoherent. The listener learns to trust the shape in miniature
before being asked to trust it across longer spans. Every use earns resolution through
perspective-shift and reconciliation, not escalation or decorative labels.

## Hub and spoke

> status: ratified (D-0055, D-0168)

Movement through complex geography: the party establishes a hub in a region, works
the surrounding troubles spoke by spoke, and eventually migrates — a root system, not
a quest-line. The pacing is built for a sprawling, multi-hundred-episode run
(D-0051): whole episodes of weather, mending, and teaching are features, not filler.
D-0168 adopts the broad-cast spoke default from campaign-006: hubs and spokes may
carry named recurring locals and their own small subplots, so long as the core four
remain the spine. A populated spoke is not dilution; at this scale it is how the
root-system form stays alive.

## The macro arc

> status: ratified (D-0014, D-0022, D-0168, D-0208, D-0210)

Three great movements, then the long tail: **sabotage** (working up the extraction
network, untying its fictions node by node), moving into **the breach** (when the
elite seal their hoards, the storyline becomes organizing and opening them), and then
**the world after** — which is not an epilogue but the point: endless rebuilding of
new societies in the ruins, new ways to live without poisonous extraction.

The binding master frame (D-0210) is **exactly four acts** and approximately 200
episodes. The total planning range is strictly 180–220 episodes, and every act is
strictly 45–55 episodes around a target of 50. No alternative act count is live.
Acts contain coherent nested arcs, but there is no canonical minimum, maximum, or
fixed number of arcs within an act. The four acts directly form the series-level
kishōtenketsu: sabotage carries Act I/ki and Act II/shō, the breach is Act III/ten,
and the world after is Act IV/ketsu. This supersedes D-0168's approximate-400
arithmetic and D-0208's eight-act interpretation while retaining their other
structural, hook, clarity, and competition findings.
The breach's perspective shift is now explicit:
the antagonist is enclosure itself — the old disease of hoard and sealed promise —
not only the current enclosers. The mission therefore changes shape from defeating a
ruling-class instance to converting hoards back into hearths and commons.

## Pre-history and exploration are threaded, not front-loaded

> status: ratified (D-0051, D-0056, D-0168)

The deep past ([[pre-history]], [[cycles]]) is revealed archaeologically along the
way — each region holding strata, ruins, and testimony that the plot must earn. The
same for the world tour itself: the widening economic and cultural lens is paced
across seasons ([[economy]], [[regions]]).

D-0168 hardens the discovery-speed guard from campaign-006: Act 1 does not contain a
major deep-time revelation. The cycles accrue slowly, one buried stratum and impossible
artifact at a time, because front-loading the deep-time truth crowds the opening arc
and fights the ratified slow assembly.

## What structure is not

> status: rejected (D-0012, D-0052)

Two dead shapes, kept as guardrails: the monster-of-the-week procession hung on one
big hunt ("isn't a story structure that feels fresh"), and the Tolkien-esque epic
quest on Freytag's pyramid — the classic, intrinsically male rising-action-to-boss
architecture. Novel plot bones or nothing.

## Episode-arc mechanics

> status: provisional (D-0072)

The working template for a spoke arc, approved directionally: arrival and friction
(ki), investigation and mapping (shō), the perspective shift — the trouble is never
what it seemed, and its cause is always human and systemic (ten), and reconciliation —
the proof spoken, the treaty rewritten, the community and land resettled (ketsu),
closing on the hearth-beat of the found family. Micro-versions of the same shape
resolve inside single episodes.

## The opening arc

> status: ratified (D-0162, D-0168)

The opening is SLOW by ruling: at least ten episodes pass before the core
configuration completes — Enfys, Aalto, Geir, and Bramble assembled in the full-team
setting — and the adventure proper begins. Each ratified meeting (the overwhelmed
meeting; the Aalto-alone Bramble bond; the late Geir reveal) gets room to land in its
own episode; the dual-pacing test's fast variants failed precisely by jamming the
last two into one. Configuration episodes between the meetings are features, not
padding (the quiet-scene counting rule, D-0152). Season arithmetic beyond the opening
arc stays the author's own design. Campaign-006's accepted center of gravity is about
fourteen episodes for the opening arc, with the rigged keep-stamped Turning deck
around episode 6 or 7 as the arc's perspective-shift engine.

## The opening

> status: ratified (D-0062, D-0113)

Episode one begins with the apprentice, alone in their world, before the protagonist
enters it; the anchor comes later. The concrete opening micro-problem is now settled
(D-0113): the apprentice, alone, re-tying a failing storm-ward knot over a sick kinsman
before the night tide — the cheap keep-stamped cord is the wrong fibre and won't seat,
salt-swollen fingers, a knot that keeps slipping, the wind rising. It is the most
audio-legible open we have, it plants the apprentice's knot-craft
([[apprentice]], D-0121) in the first minute, and the protagonist enters because of that
small competence (the plot reason for the adoption, D-0061). The ward fails because the
valley's Wyrd is souring — the parish water has been enclosed (D-0114) — and the
catastrophe that orphans the apprentice is this episode's *ten*, not its open.
